author: blu
body: No drift is expressible now, and there is no longer a second literal for one to open up against. This list is DERIVED from the emitter table, so being routed IS having an emitter, which is what routing was always supposed to mean; and the emitter table is itself derived from the one table in Types chapter Builtins, whose rows carry the name, the type and the emitter together. build/check-builtin-tables.ps1 checked the last of these relations and is deleted, because a relation between two columns of one row is not a relation any more.

author: blu
body: The emitters live over there and are named from here, which is the reverse of the usual direction and worth saying plainly: Emit sorts before Types in the concatenated unit, so `builtins` is a forward reference from this chapter. That already worked before this change, and still does in both directions: capability-vocabulary in Types is a projection of a foreword table, and boot-cap-mask-for in the X86-64 Chapter reads the same one -- so nothing here depends on a new property of the unit.

author: blu
body: Names are kept in a SkipListText, sorted by the same text-compare that skip-list-text-has uses. They arrive already ordered, since x86-builtin-emitters sorts itself for its own bsearch, and skip-list-text-from-list sorts on insert regardless. The walk binds the emitter table once: x86-builtin-emitters is a zero-parameter definition and every mention of one is emitted as a call, so naming it twice would build and sort the whole table twice. It runs where a CodegenState is built, not per is-builtin call.

author: blu
body: Two guards and both are load-bearing: delete the first and a negative index reads before the text, delete the second and any index past the end reads whatever follows. Neither can stand in for the other, so each has its own case in the tests.

author: blu
body: One guard serves Text and List alike, and it is one function rather than two because both carry their length at offset 0 and both index from zero. Two spellings of one band drift apart -- `cce-is-letter-any` spent months disagreeing with `is-letter` about where the letters were -- so the band is written once, here.

author: blu
body: The lexer's identifier scan runs through this, so the band decides which letters may appear in a name. It already accepted Tier 1 characters through their own multi-byte path, which is why the Tier 0 accented and Cyrillic band was the one thing contradicting "any language can be used in the source".

author: blu
body: That contradicted a published compliance row. `KingsAndCourts.md` carries CRA 1(a) as BY-CONSTRUCTION with "buffer overflow: no raw pointers, bounds-checked", and the ETSI and IEC matrices lean on the same row. The 2026-07-27 sweep of those documents fired every REFUSAL the compiler performs and never fired a bounds READ, which is how the row survived an audit that withdrew twenty-one of its neighbours.

author: blu
body: A fourth check, `start <= srclen`, was written first and then removed rather than shipped, because nothing could make it fire ALONE: with start and len both non-negative, a start past the end already makes srclen - start negative and no non-negative len is less than it. A guard no input can exercise on its own is the thing this tree keeps auditing out of its own test suite, and it does not get to enter through the emitter.

author: blu
body: Each of the three that remain was checked the same way and each survives. Drop `start >= 0` and start = -1 with len = 2 computes a room of six and sails through, reading before the string. Drop `len >= 0` and a negative length passes any room test and mints a Text whose length field is negative. Drop the range check and there is no bound at all.

author: blu
body: list-files and list-directories are no longer among them. They are real now, and they are not here: they live in Foreword chapter Fat16, next to file-exists and for the same reason -- the machine does not know what a directory is, and FAT16 does. So they are gone from builtin-names and from the type environment entirely, which is what lets a chapter citing Fat16 resolve them to the definitions that work. A chapter that does not cite Fat16 now gets CDX3002 on the name, which is the truth: it asked for something it did not bring.

author: blu
body: write-file and write-binary-file are no longer here either. FAT16 is not read-only any more -- it allocates a cluster, chains it, writes the bytes and commits a directory entry, all in Codex over block-write-sector -- so both names now resolve to definitions that keep their promise, next to file-exists in Foreword chapter Fat16. The emitter has nothing to say about them. write-file used to live here and print its content to the console while reporting success, which is the strongest argument in this file for why a name the compiler cannot keep does not belong in the compiler.

author: blu
body: For a while after that, the string "write-file" lingered in sorted-builtin-names with no emitter behind it. That ghost was not harmless: an application site asks is-builtin BEFORE it consults the handler table, so a `with FileSystem` handler over write-file would discharge the row at type level and then die at emit looking for an emitter that does not exist. The name is out of the list now, which is what lets the FileSystem effect's write-file op reach a handler -- the layer that services it over the disk is the one place the name resolves.

author: blu
body: Integer-width state scoped to a run-state body. State lives in a single stack-slot local whose slot index is tracked on CodegenState.state-local. Nested run-state saves and restores the slot index so inner scopes shadow, not overwrite, outer ones.

author: blu
body: The runtime half of the lane bound. CDX2093 refuses a LITERAL lane at CHECK, which is the stronger answer and the one to prefer, but it cannot see `vec-extract v i` where `i` is computed -- and every in-tree computed-lane site is a test that passes a parameter. This closes that half.

author: blu
body: char-code, code-to-char and address-of are reinterpretations and not conversions: the operand is already the value the result wants, so all three emit the first argument and nothing else. They shared one inline lambda until the table moved to Types chapter Builtins, and that move is why this function exists rather than the lambda.
